questions.q: How does PostgreSQL's user/role model differ from SQL Server's, per this lesson?
options: PostgreSQL has one unified role concept; whether it acts as a login or a permission group depends on its attributes, unlike SQL Server's separate logins and users
PostgreSQL has no concept of roles at all, only individual user accounts
PostgreSQL requires a separate user table in addition to pg_roles
SQL Server and PostgreSQL use an identical unified role model
questions.explain: PostgreSQL uses a single role object for both what SQL Server calls logins/users and roles/groups, distinguished only by attributes like LOGIN.

questions.q: What is CREATE USER in PostgreSQL, per this lesson?
options: Shorthand for CREATE ROLE ... WITH LOGIN, creating the same kind of object as CREATE ROLE
A completely separate SQL command creating a different object type than CREATE ROLE
A deprecated command with no effect in current PostgreSQL versions
A command that only works inside pgAdmin, not psql
questions.explain: CREATE USER creates exactly the same underlying role object as CREATE ROLE WITH LOGIN — there is no separate user object type.

questions.q: What does the LOGIN attribute control on a PostgreSQL role, per this lesson?
options: Whether the role can authenticate and open a connection at all
Whether the role can create new tablespaces
Whether the role's password uses scram-sha-256 versus md5
Whether the role is a member of the reporting_team group
questions.explain: LOGIN is the attribute that determines whether a role can actually authenticate and connect, functionally making it a "user" in other platforms' terms.

questions.q: What does the peer authentication method do, per this lesson?
options: For local Unix-domain socket connections, it checks the connecting OS user's username against the role name instead of requiring a password
It requires a client certificate for every connection
It is the default method for all remote TCP/IP connections
It disables authentication entirely regardless of connection source
questions.explain: peer authentication matches the OS-level username of the connecting process to the PostgreSQL role name for local socket connections, without requiring a password.

questions.q: What determines which authentication method is actually used for a given connection attempt, per this lesson?
options: The matching rule in pg_hba.conf, separate from the role's own attributes
Whether the role has the SUPERUSER attribute set
The role's CREATEDB attribute
Whether the connection uses psql versus pgAdmin
questions.explain: Authentication method is determined by pg_hba.conf rules matching the connection's type, database, user, and address — not by role attributes themselves.
